newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICAN UNION CHIEF BACKS OFF WAGE HIKE DEMAND.
newsitem.headline: MEXICAN UNION CHIEF BACKS OFF WAGE HIKE DEMAND.

text.p: The head of Mexico's most powerful labour union on Monday backed off his controversial demand for an emergency wage hike, saying he had been misreported last week making threats against the government.

Leonardo Rodriguez Alcaine, head of the six-million-strong Mexican Workers Confederation (CTM), told reporters he neither demanded an emergency wage hike nor threatened the government with strikes if it did not agree to the demand.
"I never said we were going to solicit an emergency wage hike. I said it was important to raise wages in a sustained way," Rodriguez said.

"And I didn't say that we would take to the streets (if the government did not agree to the hike). This worries me because today I was looking over what I said and I think you all twisted my comments," he added.
Last week, Alcaine surprised observers when he told reporters that the normally pro-government CTM was demanding higher wages and would back up its talk with protests.
But on Monday, Alcaine said his group would only "request" a wage hike for workers from the government and business leaders based on productivity and other incentives that would not cause inflation.
He admitted, however, that he had been "bawled out" by the government for being "indiscreet" in last week's comments.

Voices calling for a hike in the minimum wage have grown since the economy began to recover this year from the 1994-95 peso crisis. During the recent recession, the CTM leadership clamped a lid on labour protests to avoid chaos for President Ernesto Zedillo as he applied austerity measures.
